# Jlisten2me Journal, full text

> Jlisten2me is a confidential one-hour listening service in Austin, Texas, by phone or in person. Not therapy, not coaching. Nothing recorded, no notes kept.

Every published journal article, newest first. None is drawn from a session.

## When you're getting divorced and your friends are picking sides

URL: https://jlisten2me.com/journal/friends-picking-sides/
Published: 2026-10-20
Author: JFeelgood

The group chat went quiet around the time the paperwork started.
The weekend barbecue happened anyway, and you saw the photos afterward.
A couple you've known for years still texts your ex on birthdays and hasn't texted you at all.
On the weekends the kids are at the other house, the hours stretch out with nobody to fill them.

Divorce changes who you live with, and then, more slowly, it changes who calls. Some friends pull back because they don't know what to say and are afraid of saying the wrong thing. Some heard your ex's version first and settled on it before you'd said a word. And in a circle built around couples, you've become the odd number at the table.

## Why the people around you can't hold it

Mutual friends are the obvious ones to talk to, and the riskiest. Anything you say can reach your ex by the weekend, sometimes word for word, sometimes worse. Even the ones who mean well get asked, and most of them are bad at pretending they haven't heard anything.

The friends who stayed close tend to make every conversation about the divorce. You meet for a drink, and within five minutes it's the lawyer, the schedule, the house. You're grateful they ask. You'd also like one evening where you get to be a person instead of a case file.

Family has feelings about your ex too. Some relatives are angry on your behalf, and their anger becomes one more thing you have to manage. Others were fond of your ex and still are, and you can hear them working to stay neutral. Either way, you end up editing what you say before you say it.

Your lawyer is on your side, and your lawyer bills by the hour. Their job is the case. Spending a billable hour on the birthday dinner nobody invited you to makes no sense to either of you, so you hold that part back.

That leaves the loneliest part of the whole thing, the part about who's still in your life, with nowhere to go.

## Saying it to someone outside the circle

Losing friends in a divorce is a strange, slow kind of grief. It happens through silence: a missing invite, a slower reply, a conversation that stops when you walk in. Saying it out loud gives it edges. You can name the people one at a time, say what each of them meant to you, and hear how much of your ordinary week went with them.

It also matters to talk to someone who has heard nothing from your ex. There's no version of the story to correct and no impression to defend yourself against. You get to tell it from the beginning, in your own words, to someone with no side to pick and no reason to repeat it.

You can say the unflattering parts too: the hurt at being left out, the anger at a friend who should have known better, the relief about one or two who drifted. Those are hard to say to anyone who might be at the next party.

## What the hour looks like here

You can talk by phone from anywhere, or meet in person in Austin on a Wednesday at noon, at a public spot we agree on after you book. A first name is enough. Stripe takes the payment, so I never see your card.

At the start, you tell me whether you want to be talked up or want to let it out. On a weekend with the house empty, either one is a reasonable choice. I don't give advice unless you ask for it out loud. Silence is fine.

I don't take notes and nothing is recorded. I don't know your ex or anyone in your circle, and nothing you say is repeated or ever used as an example.

## Who's better for the rest

An hour of being listened to won't repair friendships, and it has nothing to do with how your divorce turns out. Your lawyer is the person for the case itself, and anything about custody, money, or what you should or shouldn't say publicly belongs with them. If you want steady support through the months ahead, a therapist or a divorce support group can offer it over time, with the same people week after week.

If you're in crisis, call or text 988 in the US.

If you'd like an hour with someone who hasn't heard either side, a phone hour is $60, booked under a first name. Pick a time.

## When you have to decide and can't tell anyone yet

URL: https://jlisten2me.com/journal/decision-you-cant-share/
Published: 2026-10-13
Author: John Parsons

You know the number before anyone else does.
Maybe it's runway: eleven months on the spreadsheet, closer to seven once you stop being generous with the forecast.
Maybe it's a list of names.
Maybe it's an offer for the company, sitting in your inbox while you decide whether to answer it.
Whatever it is, you're holding it alone, and you'll keep holding it until you know what you're going to do.

That stretch between knowing and deciding wears you down in a particular way. You walk into Monday's meeting with a level face. You answer "how's it going" with "busy." You get home, someone asks how your day was, and you pick the version that won't keep them up.

## Why the usual people can't take it

Every person you'd normally talk to has a reason they can't hear this one yet.

Your team would hear it as a forecast. Mention to your head of engineering that you're worried about spring payroll, and by Thursday two good people have quietly updated their résumés. That's a sensible reaction to what you told them, and it's exactly why you can't tell them until you've decided.

Your cofounder or partners have money and years in this too. Bring them a doubt and they'll bring their own position to it. You wanted to think out loud, and twenty minutes later you're negotiating.

Your board and investors are the people you'll eventually owe a plan. Show up with an open question and they'll hear a leader who's wobbling. Some of them will start making their own calls before you've made yours.

Your spouse or partner will listen. They always do. Then they'll carry it with you, at two in the morning, on top of everything they already carry. Most people in your seat stop bringing it home after the first few times they see that happen.

Friends in your industry know people who know your people. Austin is a small town once you're a few years into any field.

Advisors, coaches, and lawyers are useful, and you'll need some of them. They're also paid to move you toward an answer. Some days what you need is to hear what you think before anyone moves you anywhere.

## What saying it out loud does

Inside your head, a decision like this loops. The same three options come around, the same worst case, the same line you'd use in the all-hands. Looping feels like thinking, and it can go on for weeks.

Saying it to another person forces it into order. You have to start somewhere, and where you start tells you something. You hear which part you rushed past. You hear yourself argue for the option you thought you'd already ruled out. Sometimes you hear that you made the call a while ago and have been waiting for someone to let you say it.

The other person barely has to do anything. They have to stay quiet, keep up, and have no reaction that matters to you. That combination is hard to find in your own life, because everyone in your life is connected to the outcome.

## What the hour looks like

You book a time, by phone from anywhere or in person in Austin on a Wednesday at noon. You can book under a first name. Stripe handles the payment, so I never see your card.

When the call starts, you say whether you want to be talked up or want to let it out. If you'd like a question or two back, ask, and you'll get them. Then you talk. You can start in the middle. You can spend twenty minutes on the spreadsheet and ten on how you feel about the people on the list. Silence is fine.

I don't take notes and nothing is recorded. I'm not on your cap table, I don't work in your industry, and I don't know your investors. When the hour ends, the only person who leaves with any of it is you.

## What it won't do

An hour of being listened to won't make the decision for you, and it won't make it right. If you're working out severance, notice periods, or what you're allowed to tell employees, you need an employment lawyer. If it's the numbers themselves, you need your accountant or CFO. If the weight has turned into weeks of bad sleep, or into something you can't shake when the work is done, a licensed therapist is the right person, and I'll say so plainly if it comes up.

If you're in crisis, call or text 988 in the US.

If you're carrying one of these right now, a phone hour is $60 and you can book it under a first name. Pick a time.
